```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = NA)
```

This tutorial introduces to data augmentation with the package `housepi`. We'll walk through the process of associating augmented variable to individuals to then proceed with standard model generation and inference. 

## Estimate Incubation Periods Distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a database which is not a household survey. Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate the respective parameters augmenting the exposure and onset times, modeled as uniformly distributed in the reported ranges. 
We associate a positive status to all individuals and we correct for right censoring modifying the maximum values as follows:

```{r}
delays <- read.csv("delays.csv")
delays[["exposure_max"]] <- delays[["exposure_max"]] + 1 - 1e-5
delays[["onset_max"]] <- delays[["onset_max"]] + 1 - 1e-5
delays[["status"]] <- 1
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(head(delays))
```

We generate the model as showed in the [walkthrough](walkthrough.html):

```{r}
# generate the model
hemi_1 <- housepi::HouseholdModelClass("example_augm_delay_incubation")

# gamma distribution parameter definitions
hemi_1$param.append(list(
  shape = list(prior = "unif", args = list(min = 0, max = 5),
               rule = "norm", rule_args = list(sd = 1)),
  scale = list(prior = "unif", args = list(min = 0, max = 5),
               rule = "norm", rule_args = list(sd = 1))
  ))

# general setup (FIXME)
setup_1 <- list(num_iter = 100000, num_adapt = 2500, burn_in = 10000,
              thinning = 10, seed = 4815162342, num_chains = 1)
```

### Build Augmented Variables

Similarly to parameter definitions, for augmented variables we provide definitions with the models and proposer rules needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo. However, augmented variable definitions are more delicate, since they can depend on data or parameters. We state which value should be imported from data formatting it as a string "<value-name>`@D`". Here we associate to each individual an exposure and an onset time.

```{r}
hemi_1$augm.append(list(
  # define 'exposure' time
  exposure = list(
    x = "exposure_min@D", # start from data 'exposure_min'
    model = "unif",                      # associate a uniform model
    args = list(min = "exposure_min@D",  # within the range 'exposure_min' 
                max = "exposure_max@D"), # and 'exposure_max'
    rule = "norm",              # choose normal rule for the Monte Carlo
    rule_args = list(sd = 0.25) # with a std. dev. of 0.25
  ),
  
  # define 'onset' time
  onset = list(
    x = "onset_max@D", # start from 'onset_max'
    model = "unif",    # ...
    args = list(min = "onset_min@D", 
                max = "onset_max@D"),
    rule = "norm",
    rule_args = list(sd = 0.25)
  )
))

# associate data and other definitions
hemi_1$build(data = delays)
```

*Note:* The warning is telling us that the database has been interpreted as composed of single individuals, i .e. living in separate households.

We run the inference and we extract the results as usual:

```{r}
mcmc_trace_1 <- hemi_1$infer()
coda::traceplot(mcmc_trace_1, col="#0E86D4")
results_1 <- summary(mcmc_trace_1)
```

## Augment Onset Times

For a more realistics example, we use the template model "augm_onset_single_intr", where surveys are conditioned on single introduction and follow the times of onset. 
For simplicity the model assumes no asymptomatic cases. 

```{r}
hemi_2 <- housepi::HouseholdModelClass("augm_onset_single_intr")
```
This time we load the parameter definitions directly from the model template. 

```{r}
hemi_2$param.template()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(head(par_2$df)) # FIXME
```

We propose the following definitions for the augmented variable 

```{r}
# add 'onset_date'
hemi_2$augm.add(name = "onset_date",
                init_rand = TRUE,
                model = "lnorm",
                args = list(meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.5),
                range = list(max = 365))

# add 'incub_period'
hemi_2$augm.add(name = "incub_period", 
                init_rand = TRUE,
                model = "gamma", 
                args = list(shape = "inc_shape@P", 
                            scale = "inc_scale@P"),
                range = list(max = 14))

# assign model arguments of incubation period from parameters
# we use the inferred values from the first example
hemi_2$param.add(name = "inc_shape", 
                 x = results_1$statistics["shape", "Mean"])
hemi_2$param.add(name = "inc_scale", 
                 x = results_1$statistics["scale", "Mean"])

# build the model
hemi_2$build(data = "survey.csv", setup = list(seed = 17))
```

### Simulate an Outbreak

We run a simulation with the method `simulate`.

```{r}
# override status of the dataset according to simulation 
hemi_2$simulate()

# show a summary of the current dataset 
hemi_2$show_summary() # FIXME
```

In addition to the final status, the simulation associates the values of the augmented variables: the incubation period and the onset time.
This simulation, as all templated models, do not simulate a sampling process.

```{r}
# remove incubation period from simulated data
df <- subset(hemi_2$data(), select = -c(incub_period) )

# change all onsets after 9 PM to next day
is_infec <- df$status == 1
df[is_infec, "onset_date"] <- sapply(
  df[is_infec, "onset_date"], 
  function(x) if ((x %% 1) > 0.875) ceiling(x) else floor(x)
  )
```

### Validate the Simulation

We can check that inference returns the parameters used for the simulation.

```{r}
# new augmented definitions for the inference
hemi_2$augm.clear()

# add 'onset_date' definition
hemi_2$augm.add(name = "onset_date",
                x = "onset_date@D",
                rule = "norm", rule_args = list(sd = 0.5),
                rule_from = "onset_date@D")

# add 'incub_period' definition
hemi_2$augm.add(name = "incub_period",
                init_rand = TRUE,
                model = "gamma",
                args = list(shape = "inc_shape@P", scale = "inc_scale@P"),
                rule = "gibbs",
                range = list(max = 14))

# the number of iterations has been limited for brevity
setup_2 <- list(num_iter = 8000,  burn_in = 2000, thinning = 10, 
                num_adapt = 2000, seed = 57)

hemi_2$build(data = df)

mcmc_trace <- hemi_2$infer()
```

```{r}
coda::traceplot(mcmc_trace, col="#CA1F63")
results_2 <- summary(mcmc_trace)

# collect the information for the check
imask <- par_2$df["infer"] == TRUE
inames <- par_2$df[imask, "name"]
data.frame(Expec = par_2$df[imask, "value"],
           Estim = results_2[["statistics"]][inames, "Mean"],
           CI2.5 = results_2[["quantiles"]][inames, "2.5%"],
           CI97.5 = results_2[["quantiles"]][inames, "97.5%"])
```
